introduction: These readings see pairing at the root of things: the world came into being from the meeting of an active force and its recipient; the creative word 'Be' is two letters joined; Will and Purpose are called father and mother of all things; plants, animals and human beings are created in pairs for companionship; and masculine and feminine are said to belong to bodies and not to the spirit. Each of the forty quotations is read here beside one from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: 'Be! and it is', Genesis's male and female and its two great lights, the Qur'an's pairs, the Tao that produced Two, Blake's contraries, Shelley's 'nothing in the world is single', Aristotle. Four push back or add a side: Wollstonecraft on what such symbols have been made to mean for women, Aristophanes' comic tale of the other half, Heraclitus's war as father of all, and Spinoza.
questions: The readings say that existence came from the meeting of an active force and one that receives. Where in nature or in your own work do you see something new come from such a meeting?

One reading says that masculine and feminine are characteristics of bodies and have nothing to do with the spirit; another uses Adam and Eve as symbols of an active and a receptive reality. How should the two be read together, and what does Wollstonecraft's warning add?
All things are created in pairs 'in order that they might find companionship'. What does that say about solitude and about marriage?
Heraclitus calls the meeting of opposites war; Blake calls contraries necessary to progress. Which word fits the readings better?

outside.why: Blake wrote that without contraries is no progression: attraction and repulsion, reason and energy are necessary to human existence.
The Qur'an says that His command, when He intendeth a thing, is only that He saith unto it: Be! and it is.
The psalm says: he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast.
In Proverbs wisdom, spoken of as she, says that she was with the Lord in the beginning of his way, before his works of old.
The Tao Teh King counts: the Tao produced One, One produced Two, Two produced Three, Three produced all things.
Emerson says that every natural fact is a symbol of some spiritual fact.
Genesis says that in the day God created man, male and female created he them, and called their name Adam.

Mary Wollstonecraft wrote: strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience. What happens to symbols of an active and a receptive principle when they are read as descriptions of men and women?
Paul says that there is neither male nor female, for ye are all one.
Tennyson wrote that the woman's cause is man's: they rise or sink together, dwarfed or godlike, bond or free.
The Qur'an gives glory to him who created all the pairs, of that which the earth groweth, and of themselves, and of that which they know not.
Genesis has God say: it is not good that the man should be alone.
The Qur'an counts it among God's signs that he created helpmeets, and ordained between them love and mercy.
The Song of Solomon has the lover say: my beloved is mine, and I am his.
Jesus says that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, and that the two shall be one flesh.

In Plato's Symposium Aristophanes tells a tale in which each of us is the half of an original whole, always looking for his other half. He tells it as comedy. How literally should an answer about souls created in pairs be taken?
Shelley says that nothing in the world is single: all things by a law divine in one spirit meet and mingle.
Paul says that that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural, and afterward that which is spiritual.
Paul writes that by him were all things created, visible and invisible, and that by him all things consist.
Genesis tells the first act of creation in one sentence: and God said, Let there be light: and there was light.
The Qur'an calls God the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who saith unto a thing only: Be! and it is.
The psalm says that by the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth.
Proverbs says that heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop, but a good word maketh it glad.
Heraclitus said, in one of the fragments that survive of him, that the way up and the way down is one and the same.
John's Gospel opens: in the beginning was the Word, and all things were made by him.
Proverbs says that the lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof is of the Lord.
The Preacher says that two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labour.
Aristotle says that the final cause produces motion as being loved, while all other things move by being moved.
Heraclitus said that war is the father of all and the king of all. Is the meeting of an active force and its recipient a strife, as he thought, or a union?
Dante ends his poem with the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
Genesis says that God made two great lights, the greater to rule the day and the lesser to rule the night.
Plato's physician says that one ought not to attempt to cure the part without the whole, nor the body without the soul.
Isaiah asks who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and weighed the mountains in scales.
The letter to the Hebrews says that the worlds were framed by the word of God.
Paul speaks of God, who calleth those things which be not as though they were.
The psalm says of all creatures that they wait upon God, who opens his hand and they are filled with good.
Aristotle held that coming-to-be is a change into contraries and out of contraries.
Marcus Aurelius tells himself to regard the universe constantly as one living being, with one substance and one soul.
The same book says that all know the beauty of the beautiful, and in doing so have the idea of what ugliness is.

Spinoza held that all things which are, are in God, and without him can neither be nor be conceived. Is this the doctrine the passage condemns, and what does a relation through the Will put in its place?

genesis-not-good-to-be-alone.text: And the Lord God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him

matthew-twain-shall-be-one-flesh.text: Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder

genesis-male-and-female-created-he-them.text: This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, in the likeness of God made he him; Male and female created he them; and blessed them, and called their name Adam, in the day when they were created

plato-looking-for-his-other-half.text: so ancient is the desire of one another which is implanted in us, reuniting our original nature, making one of two, and healing the state of man. Each of us when separated, having one side only, like a flat fish, is but the indenture of a man, and he is always looking for his other half
plato-looking-for-his-other-half.author: Plato

blake-without-contraries.text: Without Contraries is no progression. Attraction and Repulsion, Reason and Energy, Love and Hate, are necessary to Human existence
blake-without-contraries.author: William Blake
blake-without-contraries.work: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
